📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AWS Secrets Manager now supports managed external secrets for Auth0, Okta, and Palo Alto Networks. Long-lived credentials that are not rotated increase the risk of unauthorized access if exposed. Rotating a third-party credential requires coordinated updates to the external service and every application that uses it. You set a rotation schedule from the AWS Management Console or API. Secrets Manager rotates the credential and stores the current value without a custom rotation Lambda function.

Secrets Manager offers self-rotation and administrator-assisted rotation for Auth0 credentials. With self-rotation, the target application replaces its own secret. With administrator-assisted rotation, a separate Auth0 application with Management API permissions replaces the target application's secret. For Okta, Secrets Manager offers administrator-assisted rotation with a separate administrator JSON Web Token (JWT) key and validates the replacement before deactivating the old secret. For Palo Alto Networks, Secrets Manager offers self-rotation, in which the current API key authorizes its replacement.

Applications that already retrieve credentials from Secrets Manager receive the rotated value without a code change or deployment.

These integrations join existing managed external secrets support for BigID, Cisco Security Platform, Confluent Cloud, Databricks, Datadog, GitLab, Jenkins, MongoDB Atlas, Netskope, Paddle, Salesforce, Snowflake, SonarQube, and Twilio.

Auth0, Okta, and Palo Alto Networks managed external secrets are available in all AWS Regions where AWS Secrets Manager managed external secrets is supported. To learn more, visit the  AWS Secrets Manager managed external secrets documentation .

#366. When will humans actually fly on Starship?

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

When will humans actually fly on Starship?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (958 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the stunning return of Starship from the skies to a launch tower in South Texas answered some questions about the future of SpaceX’s ambitious rocket program.
  • For example, as Starship becomes fully reusable, when might humans fly on the vehicle?
  • In a recent development, the short answer is pretty simple: If SpaceX prioritizes human spaceflight on Starship, it could happen reasonably swiftly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the stunning return of Starship from the skies to a launch tower in South Texas answered some questions about the future of SpaceX’s ambitious rocket program. Namely, it is now rapidly moving toward rapidly reusable launch.

However, it raises other questions. For example, as Starship becomes fully reusable, when might humans fly on the vehicle?

In a recent development, the short answer is pretty simple: If SpaceX prioritizes human spaceflight on Starship, it could happen reasonably swiftly. The longer answer becomes more complicated and depends on what one means by human spaceflight. The first people to fly on Starship probably won’t launch from Earth, or land here. Rather, they will probably be NASA’s lunar astronauts. So there are different timelines for humans flying aboard Starship and landing on Earth.

Given what is known publicly, and what Ars has heard privately, here are some educated guesses about all of this.

The first thing we can say for sure is that all estimates of human spaceflight on Starship should be taken with a gigantic grain of salt, including those in this article. Putting humans on any space vehicle is a difficult and time-consuming task, even outside of the requirements that NASA would impose for its astronauts.

Recent findings suggest that the original target for launching humans on Starship (then known as the Interplanetary Transport System) set a decade ago was 2024. That was for a Mars mission. Then, in 2018, SpaceX announced a lunar flyby mission on Starship with a target launch in 2023. This dearMoon mission was canceled in 2024. In 2022, SpaceX and Dennis Tito announced a lunar flyby mission later in the 2020s.

Sources indicate that more recently, according to sources, SpaceX has been telling individuals interested in launching on Starship that it could begin offering flights by 2029. I probably would not put too much stock in this date.

All of this is to say, we cannot learn much from history other than to deeply discount any public launch dates on Starship for humans.

Most likely, the first humans to fly on Starship in space will do so after launching from Earth inside the NASA Orion spacecraft. Once in orbit they will then dock with Starship before transiting to the Moon, landing there in Starship, launching from the Moon back to Orion, and then returning to Earth inside NASA’s spacecraft.

NASA signed an agreement with SpaceX to develop Starship as this “Human Landing System” in 2021, with a lunar landing targeted for 2024. To no one’s surprise, this target has moved to 2028, and there remains considerable uncertainty about the viability of this date.

Recent findings suggest that nevertheless, the success of Saturday’s tower catch should help propel the Starship program toward a higher launch cadence, which is essential for lunar missions. It therefore seems plausible, but not certain, that humans could land on the Moon inside Starship before the end of this decade.

Again, how soon SpaceX achieves this target will depend upon its prioritization of a Human Landing System, among its other major goals to accomplish with Starship. At this point, SpaceX appears to be more focused on revenue-generating activities such as launching Starlink, and eventually, Starmind data center satellites.

Much has been made about the fact that Starship does not have a launch abort system—a feature of most human spacecraft that allows a crew vehicle to be rapidly pulled away from an exploding rocket.

It has been revealed that this may not matter should SpaceX conduct its own human spaceflight missions. Unlike NASA, which imposes detailed human-rating requirements on vehicles carrying its astronauts, the Federal Aviation Administration does not certify commercial spacecraft as safe for passengers, instead operating under a regulatory framework that emphasizes informed consent and protection of the uninvolved public. Should SpaceX reach the point where it can launch Starship reliably, it will have the confidence it needs to press forward with human flights. Conceivably, this could happen within a few years.

According to potential customers, SpaceX is developing variants of the Human Landing System Starship for human flights, potentially carrying a few dozen people to the Moon. And such a prospect is tantalizing, for the interior of Starship’s pressurized cabin is almost unimaginably large for a spacecraft. A single Starship lunar lander has a pressurized habitable volume greater than the comparable volume of the International Space Station. This would be extraordinary.

Yet it is not a simple step to go from the current lunar lander design to an Earth lander. NASA’s lunar lander will never need to experience the tremendous heating of atmospheric reentry or perform the dramatic flip maneuver and propulsive landing that Starship uses to return home. Certifying those capabilities for human passengers, particularly on a vehicle without a traditional launch escape system, is an entirely different challenge.

Moreover, building a commercial human spaceflight business on Starship would be time-consuming and would likely not be nearly as profitable as launching Starlink satellites into space. And the risk is far greater—spaceflight remains dangerous, and the loss of a human crew would be a major negative for a publicly traded company. On the other hand, losing dozens of Starlink satellites on an errant launch would be a blip.

Recent findings suggest that despite Starship’s enormous theoretical capacity, SpaceX has also shown little interest in developing it as a crew transportation vehicle for commercial space stations in the near term. Several private space station operators have approached SpaceX about the possibility of Starship bringing astronauts to and from their stations. SpaceX indicated it was not interested.

Putting all of this together, I would not expect humans to land on Earth in Starship before 2030, and plausibly not until at least the mid-2030s.

Sources indicate that AWS Marketplace Metering Service now supports decimal usage quantities in the MeterUsage and BatchMeterUsage APIs. Previously, AWS Marketplace sellers reported usage to both APIs in whole numbers, and now they can report usage with up to six decimal places.

Sellers can price and meter in the units that match how customers consume their product, for example reporting 1.5 terabytes (TB) of storage instead of 1 or 2 TB. To report decimal quantities, sellers use the new UsageQuantityAsDecimal parameter in MeterUsage and QuantityAsDecimal parameter in BatchMeterUsage, and existing integrations that report whole numbers continue to work without changes. Usage allocations, which split reported usage into buckets by tags, also support decimal quantities with the new AllocatedUsageQuantityAsDecimal parameter.

This new feature is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Marketplace Metering Service is available. To learn more, see MeterUsage and BatchMeterUsage in the AWS Marketplace API Reference.

Supreme Court keeps injunction against DEI grant defunding in place

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (460 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Monday, the Supreme Court confirmed it would not hear an appeal of a lower court decision that blocked the government from canceling the grants of a handful of researchers whose funding had been revoked during the Trump administration’s purge of DEI-related work.
  • The Supreme Court provided no discussion of its rejection, and no justices filed a dissent regarding the decision.
  • Sources indicate that the suit was initially filed by a large group of researchers at the University of California, Berkeley and UC San Francisco, contesting grants originally issued by many federal agencies, from the National Institutes of Health to the Department of Transportation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Monday, the Supreme Court confirmed it would not hear an appeal of a lower court decision that blocked the government from canceling the grants of a handful of researchers whose funding had been revoked during the Trump administration’s purge of DEI-related work. While the decision applies to only seven researchers in California, the lower court had ruled that the government’s actions violated the First Amendment and so may have broad implications.

The Supreme Court provided no discussion of its rejection, and no justices filed a dissent regarding the decision.

Sources indicate that the suit was initially filed by a large group of researchers at the University of California, Berkeley and UC San Francisco, contesting grants originally issued by many federal agencies, from the National Institutes of Health to the Department of Transportation. At matter were grants that had been terminated because the agencies decided they violated a Trump executive order blocking the use of DEI. This occurred despite the fact that the government hadn’t bothered to define DEI, and targeted grants were often identified by little more than a keyword search.

In the wake of a Supreme Court decision that held that most grant termination cases had to be heard by a different court, the case was narrowed considerably to just seven UC researchers and a handful of agencies: The Environmental Protection Agency, the National Science Foundation, and the National Endowment for the Humanities.

The researchers argued that the grant cancellations were viewpoint discrimination that violated the First Amendment. A District Court agreed, issuing a preliminary injunction that would restore the grants given to these researchers.

Industry observers note that that decision was upheld by a Court of Appeals panel. It ruled that, while the government has the option of eliminating grant programs that it determined were no longer appropriate, canceling individual grants that it disagreed with is an attempt at “suppression of dangerous ideas.” In support of this, it cited Supreme Court precedent regarding religious viewpoint discrimination.

The court ruled that DEI fits in this framework because it “convey[s] the viewpoint that the exclusion of historically disadvantaged groups is undesirable.” As a result, “the government has not merely exercised its power to choose the programs it funds but has instead terminated individual grants in existing programs based on the perceived viewpoints of individual speakers.”.

Assuming this case continues, the Supreme Court may find other chances to intervene. But the fact that it hasn’t done so now is striking, given that it could easily have objected to everything from the venue to the decision that the government’s actions constituted viewpoint discrimination. And its lack of intervention may be interpreted by other courts as a sign that the government’s anti-DEI efforts are on shaky legal ground.

  • Setup used to mean configuring the machine by hand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that building AI agents has become essential. Across your organization, teams want agents to handle ERP transactions, work through a claims queue, and operate the same applications your people use every day. But how do you move from experiments to production? Before an agent touches real systems and real data, you need to verify who it acted on behalf of, what it did, and whether it stayed within the limits you set. Without that visibility, the agent stays stuck in testing, and the value is never realized.

Earlier this year, we launched Amazon WorkSpaces for AI agents, extending the power and security of a cloud work environment to agents, not just people. Today, we're excited to announce new capabilities that make it even easier to operate agents confidently across your enterprise and move them from proof of concept to governed production in fewer steps. You can set up new agents or connect the ones your builders have already built, run them under your own identity providers and policies, and keep a record of everything they do. You don't need to stitch together new tools or build custom monitoring.

Setup used to mean configuring the machine by hand. Now, you can just describe what your agent needs to your AI coding assistant such as Claude Code, Codex, and Kiro. Guided by AWS MCP skills, the assistant builds the WorkSpace from defaults you can adjust. If your teams build on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, you can connect an agent directly with your AWS credentials and skip writing any agent code. Latest tools also reduce agent costs and increase accuracy by letting an agent carry out a series of actions in a single call and use the computer-use actions its model already knows.

But an agent that can work is not necessarily an agent you can trust with mission-critical work and sensitive data. This release gives you the same oversight over an agent that you have over the employees you manage. First, agents can now sign in through any identity provider (IdP) that supports OIDC, in addition to the existing SAML support. Administrators can send sign-in straight to their IdP, so people authenticate with their usual corporate credentials, and you don't build custom authentication. Second, with on-behalf-of (OBO) sign-in, an agent works as the signed-in user, with that user's existing directory identity, permissions, and Group Policies on the desktop.

Industry observers note that workSpaces now offers session replay, giving you a reviewable record of what your agent did. Session replay turns session screenshots into a video and pairs it with a plain-language transcript of the agent's actions. Both are stored in your own Amazon S3 bucket and encrypted with your own keys. Your security team can see what the agent saw, and your compliance team gets evidence to support audits.

Together, these updates help move agents out of pilots and into real production scale. Your teams can keep working the way they do today, with agents working alongside them in familiar and trusted cloud work environments. And every one of those agents is held to the same identity, policy, and audit standards as the rest of your workforce. With WorkSpaces, you can bring AI agents into your business without rebuilding decades of software or needing a separate environment to govern them.

To get started operating AI agents on WorkSpaces, visit our documentation page.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: AWS KMS now supports key sharing with AWS Resource Access Manager

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (419 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, AWS Key Management Service (KMS) now integrates with AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM), giving you a simpler and more consistent way to share KMS keys across your AWS accounts, within your organization in AWS Organizations, and with specific IAM roles and users.
  • Sharing KMS keys through RAM makes enabling cross-account access faster to set up and safer to maintain.
  • It has been revealed that this enhancement is built on upcoming AWS RAM capabilities that are available for every resource type RAM supports.

According to recent reports, AWS Key Management Service (KMS) now integrates with AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM), giving you a simpler and more consistent way to share KMS keys across your AWS accounts, within your organization in AWS Organizations, and with specific IAM roles and users. You can now let trusted parties define the access they need through reusable managed permissions in RAM, while keeping full control of your keys and key policies. To share a key, create a resource share by selecting the keys to share, choosing a managed permission, and specifying the principals. You can use AWS managed permissions for common scenarios, or customer managed permissions (CMPs) authored by you or by trusted parties such as SaaS providers and central security teams.

Sharing KMS keys through RAM makes enabling cross-account access faster to set up and safer to maintain. The trusted parties who need access to your keys can publish the policy once as a CMP, without the need for you to modify the key policies by hand. You simply fill in the values that scope it to your environment and attach it to the resource share. Your existing key policy is untouched, so you are always in control of your key as your environment grows. When a new policy version is available via an updated CMP, you decide when to apply it to your resource shares.

It has been revealed that this enhancement is built on upcoming AWS RAM capabilities that are available for every resource type RAM supports. CMPs now support multiple policy statements and additional IAM condition operators, including StringNotEquals, BoolIfExists, and ArnLike, along with the ForAnyValue and ForAllValues prefixes, so you can express precise, least-privilege access. The parameterized managed permissions lets you place a temporary placeholder in CMPs that allows each resource share owner to customize and scope down CMPs to their environment, enabling CMPs to be reused and serve many accounts. CMPs can now be published and shared across accounts, so the authors can maintain one permission, manage its versions centrally, and see every resource share that uses it, while other accounts can use it directly without keeping their own copy.

In a recent development, KMS key sharing with RAM is available in all AWS Regions where both services are available, except the Middle East (UAE) and Middle East (Bahrain). For more information, see Sharing KMS keys with AWS RAM in the AWS KMS Developer Guide and Working with shared AWS resources in the AWS RAM Developer Guide.

#361. Comcast's "fiber-powered Wi-Fi" is just cable, AT&T notes in false advertising case

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1390 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Comcast's "fiber-powered Wi-Fi" is just cable, AT&T notes in false advertising case

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1390 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AT&T on Friday accused Comcast of false advertising in a lawsuit challenging the marketing claim that Comcast’s cable broadband service and Wi-Fi are “fiber-powered.”.
  • “This case challenges Comcast’s false advertising campaign for its residential Internet service, marketed under the Xfinity brand to consumers nationwide,” AT&T’s lawsuit said.
  • While Comcast has deployed plenty of fiber throughout the US, its cable Internet service makes the final connection to homes with coaxial cable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AT&T on Friday accused Comcast of false advertising in a lawsuit challenging the marketing claim that Comcast’s cable broadband service and Wi-Fi are “fiber-powered.”.

“This case challenges Comcast’s false advertising campaign for its residential Internet service, marketed under the Xfinity brand to consumers nationwide,” AT&T’s lawsuit said. “At the center of that campaign is Comcast’s claim that Xfinity Internet and its associated Wi-Fi service are ‘Fiber-Powered.’”.

While Comcast has deployed plenty of fiber throughout the US, its cable Internet service makes the final connection to homes with coaxial cable. This results in upload speeds being far slower than download speeds.

In contrast, fiber-to-the-home service can provide symmetrical upload and download speeds. Comcast has deployed fiber-to-the-home in only small portions of its cable territory while advertising its service as fiber-powered in the majority of areas where cable makes the final connection.

AT&T’s lawsuit said that in describing its cable broadband as fiber-powered, Comcast “conveys to reasonable consumers the misleading impression that Xfinity Internet is a fiber-to-the-home service comparable to AT&T Fiber. In fact, the vast majority of Xfinity Internet runs over a hybrid fiber-coaxial (‘HFC’) network, where the critical ‘last mile’ connection to the customer’s home uses copper coaxial cable, not fiber.”.

Recent findings suggest that AT&T has its own history of ads that mislead customers about the nature of its network. It used to advertise 4G LTE service as “5GE” or “5G Evolution,” and displayed a 5GE network icon on 4G phones. AT&T claimed that its 5G Evolution ads “served to educate customers about the billions of dollars AT&T has invested to give customers an outstanding experience,” but the BBB National Programs’ National Advertising Division found the term was likely to mislead consumers into thinking they had 5G connections.

AT&T’s lawsuit stated that Comcast’s fiber-powered claim “is literally false” because the cable firm’s HFC “architecture is fundamentally different from true fiber-to-the-home services like AT&T Fiber, which deliver fiber optic cables directly to the customer’s premises.”.

Sources indicate that “Describing that service as ‘Fiber-Powered,’ ‘Powered by fiber,’ and ‘the most reliable, fiber-powered Wi-Fi’—particularly alongside Comcast’s own representations that fiber connections outperform ‘copper-based’ alternatives—is literally false or false by necessary implication,” AT&T wrote. “In that context, Comcast unambiguously conveys that Xfinity Internet is delivered to the home over fiber or is equivalent to fiber-to-the-home service, like AT&T Fiber.”.

According to recent reports, AT&T sued Comcast in US District Court for the Northern District of California, telling the court that Comcast violated US and California competition laws. AT&T alleged that Comcast’s fiber-powered advertising is a fraudulent business act or practice and an unfair method of competition.

Recent findings suggest that “Comcast should be required to restore to AT&T any and all profits earned as a result of its false and misleading advertising or provide AT&T with any other restitutionary relief the Court deems appropriate,” the lawsuit said. The lawsuit asked for a permanent injunction “requiring Comcast to cease describing its hybrid fiber-coaxial service as ‘Fiber-Powered.’”.

AT&T mentioned that even if the court doesn’t find Comcast’s advertising to be literally false, it should determine that it is “misleading because it deceives or has the capacity to deceive a substantial segment of reasonable consumers into believing that Xfinity Internet is delivered to the home over fiber alone.”.

Comcast is cutting jobs in its cable division, which for the past few years has been losing Internet customers to fiber and fixed wireless competitors. Comcast lost 144,000 residential broadband customers in Q3 2026, up from a 91,000-customer loss in the same quarter a year ago.

Comcast is struggling against cheaper Internet service providers, including fiber ISPs. Comcast co-CEO Mike Cavanagh complained in an earnings call last month that some competitors are offering what he called “irrational pricing.” Comcast CFO Jason Armstrong said fiber ISPs are offering $30 to $40 monthly broadband deals in certain markets, and he said this is irrational because deploying fiber costs $1,500 or more per home.

In December 2025, a Reddit user reported receiving a Comcast advertisement for “fiber-powered Wi-Fi” with speeds of up to 300Mbps for $40 a month before taxes and fees. The Reddit user asked what fiber-powered Wi-Fi technology is and whether Comcast provides an adapter to connect fiber to its Wi-Fi equipment.

“Trying to understand what equipment is this Wi-Fi, because I have a hard time merging radio waves with light waves. Doesn’t match any of my tech knowledge, and I’m very curious about it,” the Reddit post stated.

A person commenting in response explained that it’s still the same cable service and that “fiber-powered” is Comcast’s new marketing term to describing the existing cable-and-fiber network. “It’s marketing,” the Reddit user wrote. “Now that so many places are offering fiber to the premises, Xfinity needs to work the word ‘fiber’ into their advertising to hide the fact that they still use decades-old, unreliable, DOCSIS technology to get Internet to your home. Their backbone network is fiber, so they call it ‘fiber-powered.’”.

Recent findings suggest that AT&T previously challenged Comcast’s fiber-powered claims through the advertising industry’s self-regulatory system operated by BBB National Programs’ National Advertising Division (NAD). The NAD determined in June that Comcast accurately described its mix of cable and fiber technology in a disclosure, but that Comcast didn’t make the disclosure prominently enough.

In a recent development, in the challenged advertising, “fiber-powered” appears alongside several other claims, including pricing offers accompanied by separate disclosures. As a result, the coaxial cable disclosure does not stand out within the larger block of disclosures, reducing its prominence. NAD also noted that in certain advertisements, including the “Overview Ad,” the disclosure appears several panels away from the “fiber-powered” claim and may require consumers to scroll to view it. In addition, the advertising does not include an asterisk or other signal directing consumers to the disclosure. While the disclosure appears in readable black font against a contrasting background, NAD concluded that the disclosure should be more prominent or placed closer to the triggering claim to increase the likelihood that consumers will notice and read it.

The NAD recommended that Comcast make the disclosure “more prominent and more proximate to the ‘fiber-powered’ Wi-Fi claim as necessary to ensure that the disclosure is clear and conspicuous.” Comcast said it would comply with the decision, but AT&T’s lawsuit makes it clear that it isn’t satisfied with the current state of Comcast’s advertising. We contacted Comcast and will update this article if it provides a response.

AT&T has a similar ongoing battle against Charter, which also describes its cable Internet service as fiber-powered. Charter modified its disclosures in response to an AT&T complaint to the NAD in March, and AT&T sued Charter in August.

“Charter deceives consumers by manipulating the word ‘fiber’ in its advertising so it can tout its ‘Spectrum Fiber Broadband Network’ and hide the fact that its network mainly connects to customers’ homes using copper wire,” said the lawsuit filed in US District Court for the Northern District of Texas.

It has been revealed that charter filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit in October. “Charter’s description of Internet services delivered over an HFC network as ‘fiber-powered’ fits the definition of the word ‘powered,’ for much as computers are ‘powered by Intel chips,’ Charter’s HFC network—and the Internet service it delivers to customers—are powered by fiber,” Charter mentioned, arguing that it uses the term “to describe the critical role fiber technology plays in its HFC network.”.

AT&T’s lawsuit against Charter remarked a Spectrum commercial didn’t make it clear enough that the broadband service uses cable. AT&T wrote, “When ‘Spectrum Fiber-Powered Internet’ first appears onscreen, it is accompanied by a miniature, momentary disclosure at the bottom of the screen amid loud music and rapidly moving visual stimuli. The disclosure indicates, ‘Spectrum Internet is powered by fiber and connected to the premises by coaxial lines,’ but the voiceover does not read it aloud. That disclosure is inadequate to cure the deception caused by Charter’s ‘Fiber-Powered Internet’ claim.”.

Charter noted its disclosures are prominent enough and that it is not deceiving customers. “A tech giant bent on hiding its coaxial connection does not illustrate it, explain it in an FAQ, and disclose it on-screen in its advertising,” Charter told the court.

Disclosure: The Advance/Newhouse Partnership, which owns 14 percent of Charter, is part of Advance Publications, which owns Ars Technica parent Condé Nast.

  • The lawsuit (PDF), filed on Friday in the San Jose, California, federal court, is seeking class-action certification and lists the City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System and “all others similarly situated” as plaintiffs.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Intel is being sued by shareholders, who are accusing the chipmaker of misleading them about the impact of the PC sales slump that contributed to a drop of 28.6 percent in the price of Intel’s stock on October 30.

The lawsuit (PDF), filed on Friday in the San Jose, California, federal court, is seeking class-action certification and lists the City of Southfield Fire and Police Retirement System and “all others similarly situated” as plaintiffs. In addition to Intel, Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan and Intel’s EVP and CFO David Zinsner are listed as defendants.

The plaintiffs claim that Intel made “materially false and misleading statements and omissions” between July 23 and October 29. They are seeking unspecified compensatory damages, plus legal and other associated fees, for shareholders during that period.

In the complaint, the shareholders argue that Intel misled them by failing to disclose: the full impact that the PC market sales slump would have on Intel’s third quarter and beyond; the impact of increasing PC component prices on PC sales for Intel’s OEM and distribution partners; that Intel was dealing with substrate supply constraints that would limit its ability to meet data center CPU demand; and “that any positive impacts to Intel’s business and financial results resulting from data center construction and other aspects of the AI boom were more than offset” by the PC sales slump.

“[S]tatements regarding Intel’s business, operations, financial results, and ability to capitalize on the boom for AI-related infrastructure spending were materially false and misleading when made, and such statements did not accurately reflect Intel’s then-present business and prospects,” the law firm representing the plaintiffs, Robbins Geller Rudman & Dowd LLP, noted in a statement on Friday.

Sources indicate that on October 29, Intel confirmed what the complaint calls “disastrous” fiscal Q3 earnings. During the quarter, revenue for Intel’s Client Computing and Physical AI Group (CCPG) business declined 5 percent year over year.

At the time, Tan pointed to an “unprecedented memory crunch” and manufacturing supply shortages hurting the PC market.

The next day, Intel’s shares fell 28.6 percent in “the largest single-day price decline for Intel common stock in over 50 years,” the complaint notes.

Intel hasn’t publicly commented on the lawsuit.

  • 1/ Resolving concurrent writes for Apache Iceberg tables using Amazon Redshift.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that amazon Redshift now supports multi-statement transactions, automatic write-conflict resolution, and time travel for Apache Iceberg tables. You can run multi-step, concurrent transformation pipelines directly on Iceberg tables and audit the results, with the transaction semantics you expect from a data warehouse. This helps anyone writing to Iceberg tables at production scale. Batch jobs get all-or-nothing commits across multiple steps. Streaming and scheduled jobs can write to the same tables at the same time. Analysts, auditors, and AI agents can query a table as it existed at any point in time.

With multi-statement transactions, you group several statements in a single BEGIN…COMMIT statement and publish them as one atomic Iceberg snapshot. This means a multi-step load such as a MERGE followed by a DELETE, can be commited together as one atomic operation, are never queryable in a half-applied state, and roll back cleanly if there's a failure. Automatic conflict resolution lets concurrent writes, such as streaming inserts alongside scheduled deletes, write to the same table and commit together when their changes don't overlap, instead of failing and retrying. Time travel lets you query a table as it existed at a past point in time with AS OF TIMESTAMP. You can use it to reproduce reports, audit changes, or recover from a bad write without keeping extra copies. These capabilities are available in all AWS commercial Regions for Amazon Redshift’s provisioned RG or serverless clusters that are writing to or querying Iceberg tables.. #355. Tech Report: Amazon S3 Vectors now supports hybrid search combining vector and full text for more relevant search results

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (352 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Amazon S3 Vectors now supports hybrid search combining vector and full text for more relevant search results

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (352 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon S3 Vectors now supports hybrid search that combines vector similarity search with full-text search within a single query.
  • S3 Vectors is designed to provide the same elasticity, durability, and availability as Amazon S3, and it reduces the total costs of storing and querying vectors by up to 90% compared to alternative vector solutions.
  • It has been revealed that hybrid search is available today in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon S3 Vectors is available, and in the AWS China Regions.

Amazon S3 Vectors now supports hybrid search that combines vector similarity search with full-text search within a single query. By combining semantic meaning and exact term matching into a single ranked list of results, hybrid search captures both intent and precise terms for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), agent memory, and search applications. This can deliver more relevant ranked results than either method alone. Hybrid search works with the same S3 Vectors APIs and maintains subsecond latency for infrequent queries and latency around 100 milliseconds or less for frequent queries.

S3 Vectors is designed to provide the same elasticity, durability, and availability as Amazon S3, and it reduces the total costs of storing and querying vectors by up to 90% compared to alternative vector solutions. With hybrid search, customers can now store the data that they want to make full-text searchable alongside the vectors. Customers write data with the PutVectors API as they do today and include the searchable text as another metadata field. S3 Vectors then automatically indexes that field for full-text search with BM25 relevance scoring. By default, S3 Vectors uses a language-agnostic text analyzer to index this data which works across most languages, and customers can optionally select a language-specific analyzer for more accurate language-aware matching. To perform a hybrid query, customers send their query text strings alongside their query vector in a single QueryVectors call; S3 Vectors runs both a vector search and a full-text search, fuses the two with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), and returns a single ranked list of the top K requested results. Customers can also run full-text and vector queries separately to apply own ranking logic, search across multiple text fields in a single query, and enable full-text search on existing data in place.

It has been revealed that hybrid search is available today in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon S3 Vectors is available, and in the AWS China Regions. To get started, use the AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or the Amazon S3 console. To learn more, visit the Amazon S3 Vectors documentation, and the Amazon S3 pricing page for pricing.

#354. Hyperscale data centers use 2% of US electricity

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (701 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Hyperscale data centers use 2% of US electricity

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (701 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, one flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on large language models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers.
  • A new study has tallied energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating in the United States between May 2024 and April 2025.
  • In a recent development, the team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, one flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on large language models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to initiative how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built.

A new study has tallied energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating in the United States between May 2024 and April 2025. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference to track moving forward.

In a recent development, the team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts.

According to recent reports, in a way, that makes this a very conservative estimate, since 272 facilities believed to be large data centers were left out. But if you’re interested in AI data centers, specifically, it’s also true that some of the facilities included may not fall in that category.

Recent findings suggest that that fact also introduces some uncertainty in the actual power usage of these data centers. Relying on other research, they use a range—some conventional data centers run at an average of about 48 percent of capacity, while AI training loads have been running higher, at around 70 percent.

Sources indicate that putting that together, the total power usage for the year by these 403 data centers was estimated at 68 to 99 terawatt-hours. That amounts to 1.5 to 2.2 percent of total US electricity use, on par with the total used by Wisconsin or Indiana.

It has been revealed that A recent Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report estimated the total electricity use of all data centers of any kind in the US (minus crypto mining) at 76 terawatt-hours in 2018. In 2024, that number was up to 192 terawatt-hours. That means the hyperscale data centers identified by this study account for something like one-third to one-half of all data center energy use.

The researchers also wanted to estimate the greenhouse gas emissions associated with generating all that electricity. It’s fairly straightforward to get a reasonable number here—calculate the mix of generation in each data center’s region of the grid, and apply that CO2 per watt-hour rate to a data center’s electricity use.

Industry observers note that this yields 21 to 31 million metric tons of CO2 for the year. That’s around 0.5 percent of total US fossil fuel CO2 emissions.

It has been revealed that these data centers aren’t located in areas of especially clean energy—their energy mix was only slightly cleaner than the US average. About 54 percent of the electricity was generated by fossil fuel power plants (dominantly natural gas), with 25 percent from renewables, and 21 percent from nuclear.

According to recent reports, this doesn’t include any “behind-the-meter” generation on-site, though. The xAI data center in Tennessee notably ran a fleet of natural gas turbines during this study’s time period, for example. Cleanview, which describes itself as a market intelligence manufacturer, has tracked a boom in on-site generation since early 2025, including 116 current or planned data centers. While this may not affect this study’s numbers much, it is becoming increasingly significant over time.

This matters because the types of generators being used are much less efficient than utility power plants, emitting 60 to 80 percent more greenhouse gases to produce the same amount of electricity. (Conversely, if a data center built solar generation instead, it could reduce the carbon footprint of its energy.).

Although this study can’t pinpoint the energy use of AI data centers alone, repeating this analysis in subsequent years could reveal the growth related to the AI buildout—at least as long as that buildout lasts.

Sources indicate that nature Sustainability, 2026. DOI: 10.1038/s41893-026-01985-7 (About DOIs).

Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) now supports replicating image deletions and tag removals to your replication destinations. Previously, ECR replication copied images to destination regions and accounts but did not replicate deletions, requiring you to manage deletions separately in each location. With replication of deletes, your destination repositories stay consistent with the source automatically.

Industry observers note that teams running multi-region or multi-account architectures no longer need to script or manually track image cleanup across every destination. When you delete an image or remove a tag in your source registry, whether directly or through a lifecycle policy, ECR propagates that deletion to each destination in the replication rule. Replicated deletions emit EventBridge events and are recorded in CloudTrail, so you have the same visibility into deletions as you do for image pushes.

Replication of deletes is available in all AWS Regions where Amazon ECR is available, at no additional cost. To get started, revision your replication configuration in the Amazon ECR console or AWS CLI. For more information, see the Amazon ECR User Guide.

#350. Industry News: Three small failures combined to take down Microsoft 365

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (758 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Three small failures combined to take down Microsoft 365

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (758 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A hidden defect in Microsoft’s cloud gateway, dormant since July, was to blame for one of the largest outages in the tech giant’s history last week.
  • Microsoft’s preliminary report places the outage between November 12 at 16:20 UTC and November 13 at 16:10 UTC, just under 24 hours total, and additional monitoring remained in place for any affected systems through November 14.
  • The outage started on November 12 and promptly rippled through businesses and public offices that depend on Microsoft’s cloud and email exchange infrastructure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A hidden defect in Microsoft’s cloud gateway, dormant since July, was to blame for one of the largest outages in the tech giant’s history last week. A preliminary Post-Incident Report (PIR) released by the company outlines how the latent bug, changes in traffic, and reduced server capacity combined to knock much of Microsoft 365 and Exchange infrastructure offline at the end of last week. Microsoft’s report lists the incident’s final status as “a technical concern not related to cyber or AI/agents.”.

Microsoft’s preliminary report places the outage between November 12 at 16:20 UTC and November 13 at 16:10 UTC, just under 24 hours total, and additional monitoring remained in place for any affected systems through November 14.

The outage started on November 12 and promptly rippled through businesses and public offices that depend on Microsoft’s cloud and email exchange infrastructure. The outage is covered in Microsoft’s incident IDs EX1550543 and MO1550821. You need Microsoft 365 admin credentials to see the full report on the manufacturer’s status pages, but Office Watch has reproduced the preliminary report, and the University of Pennsylvania maintains an archive of Microsoft’s service-health updates.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft attributes the outage to three factors. A change deployed to Microsoft’s cloud gateway starting in July created a bug where, under certain conditions, CPU and memory resources could become exhausted and unresponsive. Microsoft contends that the defect was never discovered in pre-release testing because the hardware used was less powerful than some systems already deployed in production, where higher CPU core counts on newer machines apparently contributed to the lockout.

Industry observers note that the second factor was server load. Microsoft remarked that “Traffic shifts during standard network maintenance and upgrades exposed a latent bug.” The tech giant keeps two independent gateway systems in place to access Microsoft 365 for resilience. If one system encounters trouble and users can’t get through the front door, the other is opened to keep traffic flowing. According to the report, about 15 hours prior to the outage, traffic from Teams was shifted from the alternate gateway to the primary, where Exchange Online access is maintained. The switchover was a standard fail-safe, but it left the gateway handling more traffic, with a different mix of requests than before. As requests continued to pile up, affected servers exhausted their capacity and refused latest connection requests.

The traffic shift exposed a third factor: infrastructure capacity. An existing fault meant that Microsoft’s gateway server fleet was operating at 14 percent below optimal conditions. That missing headroom could have normally absorbed the demand, but when combined with the changed traffic patterns and underlying defect, it left the gateways with lock contention as requests kept piling up.

As US business operations began hitting their daily peaks, the gateway servers began to freeze. Backup systems that shifted requests away from unresponsive servers did their job, but were met with the same lockouts on the supposedly healthy backup gateways. This created a snowball effect, leaving more than 80 percent of Microsoft’s affected gateway servers frozen in the sweep. Mechanisms in place to isolate affected systems by region seem to have failed. Microsoft’s current report doesn’t address why these isolation systems may have failed.

Recovery took longer than normal because the fix required a targeted system update from Microsoft engineers. Attempts to restart the gateway servers were ineffective; when the servers came back online, large request queues were still waiting for access, immediately triggering the same resource exhaustion that contributed to the outage in the first place. Microsoft says that services like Teams, OneDrive, and other Office applications could be routed away from the affected infrastructure, but scaling limitations stopped Exchange Online from making a similar move.

Since the bug from July was still undiscovered, system rollbacks were equally ineffective. Simply returning to a previous state where things were “working” couldn’t happen, because the ghost was already in the machine. Servers were patched and returned to service gradually, and Microsoft indicates it has added additional capacity and traffic-distribution guardrails to try to avoid anything similar happening again. Microsoft also extended delivery timeouts on affected emails to stop delayed messages from bouncing back as undeliverable.

Sources indicate that microsoft expects to publish its full final incident report on November 20. This final report may provide additional clarification on why the regional isolation systems failed and what corrective actions will be taken to ensure this type of outage can be avoided in the future. All of Microsoft’s cloud services appeared online and operational as of Monday morning.

In a recent development, you can now allocate the storage and request costs of a shared Amazon S3 general purpose bucket to its prefixes in the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR). Many organizations store data for multiple teams, applications, or tenants in one bucket under different prefixes such as "marketing/" and "finance/". Industry observers note that with this latest capability, S3 Storage Lens publishes prefix-level storage and request metrics to AWS Billing and Cost Management. Each prefix line item carries its full prefix path as AWS-generated cost allocation tags, so you can total costs by top-level prefix, team, or application, and reconcile it back to the bucket. You can use this data for chargeback and showback, and to see which prefixes drive your S3 spend.

To get started, enable AWS Billing and Cost Management publishing in your S3 Storage Lens advanced tier configuration, then enable split cost allocation data for S3 in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) introduces resource optimization for EKS Auto Mode, a upcoming capability that rightsizes the CPU and memory requests of running Pods based on their actual usage.

Industry observers note that amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) introduces resource optimization for EKS Auto Mode, a upcoming capability that rightsizes the CPU and memory requests of running Pods based on their actual usage. CPU and memory requests are often set at deploy time and rarely revisited, and Auto Mode provisions EC2 instances to fit them. Rightsizing lets Auto Mode run the same Deployments and StatefulSets on fewer or smaller instances, without hand tuning and at no additional charge.

In a recent development, turn on resource optimization by creating a ClusterResourceOptimizationPolicy in your EKS cluster, review its recommendations in the default Recommend mode, and switch to Apply mode when you're ready to resize running Pods in place, without recreating them. For example, a platform team running Java services under Argo CD can rightsize every application namespace without editing templates or creating GitOps drift, while resource optimization keeps memory above each Java heap and raises memory after an out-of-memory kill. It doesn't change the CPU or memory that a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler or KEDA scales on, and you can exclude workloads that the Vertical Pod Autoscaler already manages.

You can use resource optimization on EKS Auto Mode clusters running Kubernetes 1.36 or later in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Asia Pacific (Seoul), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo).

To learn more, see Rightsize workloads with resource optimization in the Amazon EKS User Guide and the EKS Auto Mode product page.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that starting today, you can allocate the storage and request costs of a shared Amazon S3 general purpose bucket to the prefixes in that bucket in the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR).
  • Recent findings suggest that with Split Cost Allocation Data for Amazon S3, Amazon S3 Storage Lens publishes prefix-level storage and request metrics to AWS Billing and Cost Management, which allocates the bucket's storage and Tier 1 and Tier 2 request costs to the deepest matching prefix in the range of prefix levels you choose.
  • According to recent reports, to get started, enable AWS Billing and Cost Management publishing in an S3 Storage Lens advanced tier dashboard configuration, then enable split cost allocation data for Amazon S3 in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console.

Sources indicate that starting today, you can allocate the storage and request costs of a shared Amazon S3 general purpose bucket to the prefixes in that bucket in the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR). Organizations often store data for many teams, applications, or tenants in one bucket under different prefixes, such as `marketing/` and `finance/`. Until now, attributing that bucket's bill to each prefix required custom pipelines built on S3 Inventory or Storage Lens reports and your own pricing logic.

Recent findings suggest that with Split Cost Allocation Data for Amazon S3, Amazon S3 Storage Lens publishes prefix-level storage and request metrics to AWS Billing and Cost Management, which allocates the bucket's storage and Tier 1 and Tier 2 request costs to the deepest matching prefix in the range of prefix levels you choose. Each prefix line item carries its full prefix path as AWS-generated cost allocation tags, so you can total cost by top-level prefix, team, or application, and reconcile it back to the bucket. You can use this data for chargeback, showback, and to see which prefixes drive your S3 spend.

According to recent reports, to get started, enable AWS Billing and Cost Management publishing in an S3 Storage Lens advanced tier dashboard configuration, then enable split cost allocation data for Amazon S3 in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console. Prefix cost data appears in your CUR after the next daily Storage Lens metrics are published. Split Cost Allocation Data for Amazon S3 is available in all AWS commercial Regions where S3 Storage Lens advanced metrics are available, at no additional charge beyond S3 Storage Lens advanced tier pricing. To learn more, visit the AWS Cost and Usage Reports product page, Understanding split cost allocation data, and Estimating Amazon S3 costs by prefix with S3 Storage Lens.

#346. Artist brings old Space Shuttle tank back to life

Artist brings old Space Shuttle tank back to life

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1309 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Natalie Rosen is not the type of specialist you immediately associate with being one of the key people behind the new exhibit of the space shuttle Endeavour.
  • Industry observers note that she is not a former NASA technician or engineer, as many of her colleagues have been for the past several years, nor is she a curator or conservator.
  • Without her expertise and artistry, however, the largest component of Endeavour‘s “stack” would look nothing like it did when the shuttle was flying.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Natalie Rosen is not the type of specialist you immediately associate with being one of the key people behind the new exhibit of the space shuttle Endeavour.

Industry observers note that she is not a former NASA technician or engineer, as many of her colleagues have been for the past several years, nor is she a curator or conservator. Before this job, she had no experience working on any aircraft or spacecraft, as the latest Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center, an extension of the California Science Center, opened in Los Angeles on November 13.

Without her expertise and artistry, however, the largest component of Endeavour‘s “stack” would look nothing like it did when the shuttle was flying.

“My background is in the fine arts. I have my bachelor’s and my master’s in fine arts from Cal State Long Beach,” Rosen told collectSPACE.com. “When I came in on this project, they were looking for a sculptor, and I had been sculpting.”.

Rosen had been working with mixed media for her thesis project and had experience sculpting foam. As it happened, the California Science Center had a lot of foam that needed shaping.

Industry observers note that for those unfamiliar, the space shuttle was assembled from three primary launch components. The orbiter and its solid rocket boosters were reusable, given the time needed to inspect, service, and, in the case of the solid-fuel motors, refurbish and refill between flights.

The 154-foot-tall (47-meter) external tank was the only major part of the stack that was disposed of with each launch. After providing propellant for the orbiter’s three main engines, the tank was jettisoned and disintegrated while reentering the atmosphere.

In a recent development, to protect the orbiter from the extreme cold of the cryogenic liquid oxygen and liquid hydrogen in the external tank and to keep the propellant and oxidizer from boiling off too rapidly, the ET was covered in insulating foam. (Some of that foam became liberated during ascent and was what caused the loss of the space shuttle Columbia and its crew in 2003.).

In a recent development, the only flight-worthy tank to remain at the end of the program was ET-94. A so-called lightweight tank, it was built at a time when NASA was transitioning to a super-lightweight model and was therefore set aside. Originally slated to support a science mission on Columbia, it instead became a testbed after the tragedy, having its foam stripped off and tested to better understand what had happened.

In a recent development, after the program ended, NASA donated ET-94 to the California Science Center. It arrived by way of a transoceanic barge and a road trip, then sat at Exposition Park for nearly a decade.

“So much of the foam on the ET had been dissected and removed during its time as a test article that they [the California Science Center] were trying to figure out how to put it back on and blend it in to the original foam in a convincing way,” stated Rosen.

There has been a longstanding debate among shuttle enthusiasts and modelers about exactly what color the external tank is, and the answer resides in the foam.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s orange. It’s cream. It’s burnt sienna. It just depends on the original foam, when you’re seeing it and how it’s aging. Because it starts as a kind of very ice cream-white almost color, and then depending on how long it sits out in the Sun, it turns orange,” said Rosen.

In a recent development, by the time she had come on staff, the decision for the most part had already been made. Dennis Jenkins, the leader of the Endeavour project, had blended a special paint called “ET Orange” that was used to cover the existing acreage “bumpy” foam. Separately, a mocha-like color was picked out for the intertank.

Sources indicate that “And then the latest foam to be installed, which would have looked the newest on all of the closeout hardware—the feed lines, the ice frost ramps, the flanges around the intertank and the intertank rings—those were all the lightest color that we custom mixed. That was what we called the ice cream color,” Rosen said.

According to recent reports, it was not only about color matching, though. For multiple reasons, the original aerospace-grade foam could not be used, so a commercial substitute had to be found that could match what Rosen described as the “orange peel.”.

“If you look at the tank very closely, there’s this bumpy texture, and there is a pattern from the original manufacturing and how it was sprayed on. There’s this overlapping line, a subtle-like stripe to it,” she noted.

Replicating that pattern was not easy.

“There was a lot of trial and error in the beginning of what we could do to try and get it to match what was already there,” Rosen told collectSPACE. “We tried taking impressions off of the real foam and making molds and casting, but that didn’t really work. I then suggested we put in a dense urethane, like plain urethane foam, and I hand-sculpt the top of it to match what was around it. That ended up becoming the best solution for fixing the acreage foam that had an orange peel-like texture.”.

Jenkins, who had worked as a space shuttle engineer and led NASA’s delivery of the orbiters to their museum homes, had high praise for Rosen and her work.

It has been revealed that “She had to come up with a lot of latest processes because we couldn’t apply foam the same way they did at Michoud. It’s not flightworthy by any means, but just coming up with how to make it look real took a lot of imagination on her part, and she was pretty much a one-woman show for most of it,” he said.

In a recent development, some of the repair work to the external tank was finished before it was lifted by crane into the Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center and mated with the boosters and Endeavour. From then on, Rosen had to climb scaffolding to get to her worksites.

“It’s definitely the largest art project I’ve ever worked on, and, I mean, I touched every inch of it,” Rosen said. “Once it went vertical, I was going up and down stairs. Probably the scariest was the point in the scaffolding where it just became ladders. So I had to be very, very careful and calculated in what I was doing.”.

Sources indicate that even after the scaffolding was removed in preparation for the museum opening, Rosen’s ascents were not over. A couple of weeks ago, she had to install a final component on the aft dome of the liquid hydrogen tank. To reach that, she needed a scissor lift.

In a recent development, now that the entire Endeavour stack has made its public debut, Rosen is not parting ways with the California Science Center. Her work on ET-94 has launched her career into a latest frontier.

“In this last year, I have been working on different artifacts with the team. I have been helping leading up to the opening. I’ve helped in ways with the different aircraft, with their assembly, their disassembly, and reassembly. I’ve done some repairs in certain areas. I’ve worked with our satellite and probe collection to do repairs and also contacted specialists outside of my realm to clean and repair thermal blankets,” noted Rosen.

In a recent development, “So I’m planning on staying with the museum for now. They’ve offered me another position, and I’m happy to stay,” she said.

The California Science Center’s Samuel Oschin Air and Space Center is now open to the public. Admission is free, but timed entry tickets are needed due to the high demand. Reservations can be made online or at 213-744-2019.

Industry observers note that AWS Billing and Cost Management now gives customers symmetric, granular control over how credits, Reserved Instances, and Savings Looks are shared across their organization. Organizations with grant funding, regulatory obligations, or multi-entity structures can now automate benefit allocation that previously required manual chargeback reconciliation. With these new capabilities, customers can set default sharing preferences that automatically apply to all cost-saving benefits, and override those defaults for individual benefits when business requirements demand it.

Customers configure Credit Group Sharing through the Billing Preferences page to set a single default that every newly introduced credit inherits automatically, ending the cycle of per-credit manual configuration. For Reserved Instances and Savings Plans, customers configure sharing preferences at the individual commitment level through the Savings Plans or Reserved Instances inventory pages, whether purchased at a linked account or at the payer level. All sharing configurations use Cost Categories, the same grouping construct customers already use in Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, and the Cost and Usage Report.

These capabilities are available starting November 17, 2026, in all AWS Regions through the AWS Billing and Cost Management Console and public APIs. There is no additional charge. To learn more, visit the for documentations for Credit Group Sharing and Savings Proposal and Reserved Instances Level Sharing.

  • Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, said it is a “pivotal time” for US climate and energy policy.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

ANTALYA, Turkey—After their big gains in the 2026 midterm elections, a delegation of Democratic US House members appeared at the United Nations COP31 climate change conference Monday, pledging to rejoin the international fight against global warming.

Sources indicate that rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, said it is a “pivotal time” for US climate and energy policy.

“The wrecking ball of Donald Trump and this out-of-touch administration, and the temporarily empty chair of the United States at this COP31, does not represent what the Americans want or need,” Huffman stated.

President Donald Trump has pulled the United States out of the Paris climate agreement twice and is trying to quit the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. The current administration has also tried to cut all funding for climate programs.

Since Trump returned to the White House in 2025, the United States has had no formal government presence at the UN talks, but was informally represented by America Is All In, a coalition including local governments, businesses, faith groups, Native American tribes, and universities.

Huffman said the midterm election shows that Americans have rejected the current administration’s efforts to “turn the United States into something like a petro-dictatorship.” The results could pave the way for the country to reestablish a formal presence at the annual talks.

Given legal uncertainties about Trump’s efforts to completely withdraw the US from the UN’s climate framework, the extent of US participation in the talks is unclear. But Huffman stated that, in the past, US congressional delegations have attended the annual Conference of the Parties, as the meeting is formally known, under both Democratic and Republican majorities.

“The next time we’re here, we will be an official congressional delegation led by the leadership of the House of Representatives,” Huffman remarked in an interview with Inside Climate News.

The US would still be excluded from the formal government-to-government negotiations, but a congressional delegation representing the majority party, potentially capable of advancing climate and energy legislation, could make a difference, Huffman noted.

Recent findings suggest that “We want to take the best practices that we’ve heard from all of the global partners… and craft them into good, solid climate policy once we get back to Congress,” remarked Rep. Lucy McBath (D-Ga.).

It has been revealed that the new Democratic majority in the House of Representatives can also use its oversight authority to try to ensure that the money the US has promised for climate aid and sustainable development is restored, stated U.S. Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.).

Casten noted some of America’s European allies are “spending $500, $600 million per day more than before the United States attacked Iran” because of increased oil prices, and that simply stopping those hostilities could free up funding for climate efforts.

According to recent reports, “We have lost [the] trust of the international community when it comes to climate,” noted Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.).

“I think it is a complete betrayal of our responsibility that Donald Trump has pulled us out of the Paris Agreement not once but twice,” she said. A Democrat winning the 2028 presidential election would help ensure the US can rejoin that agreement, she added.

It will take time to regain trust in the international community, Ansari said.

“But we will come back,” she remarked, “working 10 times harder, 50 times harder than we did before, to make sure that we are being team players, to make sure that we are… supporting small island developing states and supporting vulnerable African nations.”.

Climate activists reacted cautiously to the promises about the United States’ potential return to the international climate arena.

“We welcome the political shift in the United States that puts the brakes on the reckless dismantling of domestic green policies,” mentioned Harjeet Singh, director of Satat Sampada Climate Foundation. “However, here at COP31 in Antalya, the international community cannot afford to celebrate prematurely or suffer from collective amnesia.”.

Singh stated the US has a long history of obstructing climate negotiations across successive administrations and regardless of which party holds power.

It has been revealed that “As the world’s largest historical emitter, the US carries an outsized moral and legal responsibility to act,” he remarked. “Real change will not be measured by who walks through the halls of this summit, but by whether Washington finally ends its expansion of oil, gas, and coal at home and delivers hundreds of billions of dollars in grant-based climate finance to developing countries.”.

Singh said until the US pays its fair share to help vulnerable countries recover from climate impacts and transition to sustainable energy systems, “warm words from visiting lawmakers mean very little to communities on the frontlines.”.

Brandon Wu, with ActionAid USA, said the new Democrat-led House majority must reassert control over the budget and hold the Trump administration accountable for “likely illegal actions like dismantling USAID and gutting foreign assistance” funding approved by Congress.

According to recent reports, “What they can deliver to the United Nations process is extremely limited,” he said, adding that it’s unlikely there will be any sweeping fresh climate legislation or climate funding in the next two years. What members of Congress can do is lay the groundwork for more ambitious action in a post-Trump era, he added.

While meeting delegates from other countries, Huffman said he’s heard both gratitude and optimism, as well as skepticism, about a possible US return to the climate talks.

“The fact is the US has become kind of an unreliable partner and we’ve lost our credibility,” he noted. “So we’ve tried to bring humility to this moment. We’ve got work to do to reclaim our credibility in this institution.”.

Sources indicate that bob Berwyn is an Austria-based reporter who has covered climate science and international climate policy for more than a decade. Previously, he reported on the environment, endangered species, and public lands for several Colorado newspapers, and also worked as editor and assistant editor at community newspapers in the Colorado Rockies.

This story originally appeared on Inside Climate News.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

The data is very preliminary, but Vulcan failure may not be due to BE-4 engines

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (685 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • United Launch Alliance (ULA) confirmed Tuesday morning that its return-to-flight launch of the Vulcan rocket began failing during the initial stages of the mission.
  • “While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff, the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit,” the manufacturer mentioned.
  • The launch company also confirmed reporting by Ars that the Centaur V upper stage and the solid rocket boosters performed nominally during the flight.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

United Launch Alliance (ULA) confirmed Tuesday morning that its return-to-flight launch of the Vulcan rocket began failing during the initial stages of the mission.

“While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff, the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit,” the manufacturer mentioned.

The launch company also confirmed reporting by Ars that the Centaur V upper stage and the solid rocket boosters performed nominally during the flight.

It has been revealed that critically, ULA did not provide any specific information about the “low booster performance.” This matters greatly because the core stage of the Vulcan rocket is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are provided by Blue Origin. That company’s own Upcoming Glenn rocket uses a similar but slightly more powerful version of the BE-4 engine. And New Glenn experienced its own catastrophic failure in May during a ground test, a failure that later was attributed to a main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines.

Recent findings suggest that information about the Vulcan failure is being closely held by ULA and Blue Origin, who have only acknowledged that they’re working together to investigate the cause. According to two sources, the investigation is “incredibly complicated” and remains in the early stages.

However, according to preliminary data, two independent sources indicated to Ars that the problem is currently believed to have originated on the launch vehicle side rather than in the engines themselves. The glitch may be related to systems that feed methane and liquid oxygen propellant to the engines.

ULA engineers are looking at the possibility that one of the two BE-4 engines started producing lower thrust shortly after liftoff and never ramped back up to full throttle for the remainder of the burn. Video observations from high-zoom tracking cameras appeared to show one engine slightly dimmer than the other after Vulcan jettisoned its solid rocket boosters nearly two minutes into flight. An asymmetric shutdown of the BE-4 engines could also have contributed to the sudden attitude motion indicated by ULA’s telemetry-driven real-time animation near stage separation.

Recent findings suggest that the Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the investigation, which is being led by ULA. Again, this information is preliminary, and no definitive conclusions can or should be drawn.

Sources indicate that this was the fifth flight of the Vulcan rocket since its debut in January 2024. Two of the previous flights have experienced problems with the nozzles on its solid rocket boosters, but in both cases, the rocket was able to compensate for the reduced and asymmetric thrust and reach its intended orbit. The second nozzle issue caused Vulcan to stand down for nine months.

This latest setback is likely to sideline Vulcan for at least half a year, and probably longer. Most impacted will be the US Space Force, which has national security payloads waiting for a ride to space on Vulcan, and Amazon, which had more than a dozen launches of its Amazon Leo constellation on the manifest for 2027. It would exacerbate a worsening launch crisis in the United States.

Sources indicate that there are potentially serious implications for Blue Origin as well, which is seeking to return New Glenn to flight as early as January. Last Tuesday, the organization said a modified BE-4 main oxygen valve had successfully completed qualification testing.

“Our modified valve has already been incorporated into engines slated for upcoming flights, and we are now rolling it out across the remaining fleet,” the organization said. “We expect to complete the anomaly investigation later this month.”.

Industry observers note that if Vulcan’s failure were ultimately due to a problem with the BE-4 engine, it would certainly delay the Fresh Glenn rocket’s return to flight. This would be a setback not just for Blue Origin but for NASA, which is counting on the super heavy lift rocket to do much of the heavy lifting for its Artemis Program and Moon Base.

AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) introduces Access Troubleshooter, a latest capability that gives you visibility into the full authorization context behind access denied errors so you can resolve them without trial-and-error. Previously, developers relied on the Amazon Resource Name (ARN) of the denying policy to debug a denial, with no visibility into the authorization context or other policies evaluated in the request that could contribute to the denial. This made troubleshooting access challenges time-consuming and inefficient.

Starting today, access denied error messages for supported services and APIs will include a unique identifier that you can use to retrieve details of the authorization performed by the service. You gain visibility into what policies were evaluated for each request, the authorization context of those requests, and the results of the evaluation. This enables you to identify the root cause of authorization challenges quickly, streamlining your access management workflows and reducing time spent debugging permission problems.

To learn more about Access Troubleshooter and how it can help you resolve access denied errors efficiently, see the User Guide on troubleshooting access denied error messages.
